items.stem: Explain, with the help of a fully labelled diagram, the simple two-sector circular flow of income between households and firms.
items.answer: Diagram: two boxes, households and firms. Inner loop (real flows): factors of production from households to firms; goods and services from firms to households. Outer loop (money flows): factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) from firms to households; consumption expenditure from households to firms. With no leakages or injections income = output = expenditure and the flow is constant.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: two boxes, households and firms. Inner loop (real flows): factors of production from households to firms; goods and services from firms to households. Outer loop (money flows): factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) from firms to households; consumption expenditure from households to firms. With no leakages or injections income = output = expenditure and the flow is constant. IB Paper 1(a) markbands [10]: Level 4 (9-10) terms defined; clear, focused explanation; relevant, accurate and fully labelled diagram(s) that are explained. Level 3 (6-8) mostly accurate with some development. Level 2 (3-5) limited explanation or diagram errors. Level 1 (1-2) little understanding.

items.stem: "Governments should use direct provision of services rather than cash transfers to reduce inequity." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Both are needed: services address long-run opportunity, cash addresses immediate poverty.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ensures spending on merit goods such as health and education; builds human capital and opportunity. Arguments against: cash gives people choice and dignity; transfers are quicker and cheaper to administer; evidence from cash-transfer programmes shows positive outcomes. Supported judgement: Both are needed: services address long-run opportunity, cash addresses immediate poverty. Markbands (15 marks): IB Paper 1(b)/2(d) markbands [15]: Level 5 (13-15) relevant terms defined; theory explained clearly with an accurate, fully explained diagram where relevant; appropriate real-world examples; effective synthesis and a supported evaluation (short- vs long-run, stakeholders, assumptions, priorities). Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "regulation".
items.answer: Rules imposed by the government on the behaviour of firms and consumers, such as bans, standards and licences
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: rules imposed by the government on the behaviour of firms and consumers, such as bans, standards and licences. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "Scarcity only exists when there is a shortage of a product in the shops." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Scarcity is the permanent condition of limited resources relative to unlimited wants; a shortage is a temporary situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a given price.
items.markingKey: Scarcity is the permanent condition of limited resources relative to unlimited wants; a shortage is a temporary situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a given price. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that the law of diminishing marginal returns is unimportant for modern firms that rely on technology.
items.answer: Diminishing returns still applies wherever a factor is fixed in the short run; digital goods are an important but limited exception.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: technology firms (software) have very low marginal costs; firms can quickly add capital in the cloud. Arguments against: most firms still have fixed factors in the short run (factories, land); agriculture, manufacturing and services face capacity limits; it explains rising short-run marginal costs and upward-sloping supply. Judgement: Diminishing returns still applies wherever a factor is fixed in the short run; digital goods are an important but limited exception. Reward explicit use of the extract. items.stem: With reference to Finland's basic income experiment (2017-2018), explain how it illustrates how economists test hypotheses with real-world data.
items.answer: 2,000 unemployed people received €560 a month unconditionally and their outcomes were compared with a control group. A randomised trial let researchers isolate the effect of an unconditional payment on employment and well-being, holding other factors constant by comparison with the control group.
items.markingKey: Context (2,000 unemployed people received €560 a month unconditionally and their outcomes were compared with a control group.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A randomised trial let researchers isolate the effect of an unconditional payment on employment and well-being, holding other factors constant by comparison with the control group. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how economists test hypotheses with real-world data.

items.stem: You are an economist advising the government. A minister argues that market failure is so common that governments should intervene in most markets. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: Market failure justifies targeted intervention where it is significant, not intervention in all markets.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: externalities are widespread (energy, transport, food); information problems in health, finance. Counter-points: many markets work well without intervention; government failure is also common; intervention has administrative costs. Recommendation: Market failure justifies targeted intervention where it is significant, not intervention in all markets. Policy recommendation markbands [10]: Level 4 (9-10) a clear recommendation that is justified with economic theory, the information provided and its likely consequences for stakeholders; trade-offs and risks weighed. Level 3 (6-8) recommendation supported but justification partly developed. Level 2 (3-5) limited justification. Level 1 (1-2) recommendation asserted.

items.stem: Using an appropriate diagram, explain how an indirect tax can be used to reduce the consumption of a good.
items.answer: Diagram: market for sugary drinks; specific tax shifts supply from S to S + tax (vertical distance = tax). Price paid by consumers rises from Pe to Pc, quantity falls from Qe to Qt; producers receive Pp = Pc − tax; government revenue = tax × Qt.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: market for sugary drinks; specific tax shifts supply from S to S + tax (vertical distance = tax). Price paid by consumers rises from Pe to Pc, quantity falls from Qe to Qt; producers receive Pp = Pc − tax; government revenue = tax × Qt. items.stem: "Direct government provision is the best way to increase consumption of merit goods." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Direct provision is effective for basic merit goods such as primary education, but subsidies, regulation and information can complement it more efficiently.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: guarantees access for all (equity); can achieve large increases in consumption quickly; avoids reliance on private profit motives. Arguments against: high fiscal cost and opportunity cost; possible inefficiency and lack of choice; over-consumption and waiting lists when free; subsidies or vouchers may achieve similar results at lower cost. Supported judgement: Direct provision is effective for basic merit goods such as primary education, but subsidies, regulation and information can complement it more efficiently. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "price elastic demand".
items.answer: Demand for which PED is greater than 1 (in absolute value), so quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: demand for which PED is greater than 1 (in absolute value), so quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Over one year the price of coffee rose by 40% and the quantity supplied rose by 16%. Over the same year the price of T-shirts rose by 40% and the quantity supplied rose by 48%. Calculate the PES for each product and explain the difference.
items.answer: coffee: PES = 0.4; T-shirts: PES = 1.2
items.markingKey: coffee: 16/40 = 0.4 [1]; T-shirts: 48/40 = 1.2 [1]; commodity supply inelastic because of gestation periods/fixed land or long mine lead times, manufacturing elastic because of spare capacity, stocks and factor mobility [2].

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that governments should use insights from behavioural economics to design policy.
items.answer: Behavioural insights improve policy design, but they should be transparent, tested and combined with traditional tools.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: low-cost nudges with significant effects (auto-enrolment, tax letters); policies better matched to how people actually behave. Arguments against: risk of manipulation and paternalism; effects may be small or fade; governments also have biases. Judgement: Behavioural insights improve policy design, but they should be transparent, tested and combined with traditional tools. Reward explicit use of the extract. items.stem: Factor incomes in Atlantis are: wages $477bn, rent $40bn, interest $31bn, profits $85bn. Households then decide to spend 15% less in a two-sector economy. Calculate the new value of expenditure and explain what happens to factor incomes in the next round.
items.answer: $538.05bn; factor incomes fall to $538.05bn as firms receive less revenue
items.markingKey: Income = 633; new spending = 633 × 0.85 = $538.05bn [2]; firms' revenue falls so they pay out less: incomes fall, the flow shrinks [2].

items.stem: You are an analyst at the competition and consumer authority. A minister argues that price is the most important factor influencing how much of a good consumers buy. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: Price matters for quantity demanded, but non-price determinants often cause larger changes in demand.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: the law of demand shows strong price effects for most goods; firms' pricing strategies work. Counter-points: income, tastes and the prices of substitutes can shift demand substantially; for necessities and addictive goods price has a weak effect; advertising and habits matter (behavioural economics). Recommendation: Price matters for quantity demanded, but non-price determinants often cause larger changes in demand. Policy recommendation markbands [10]: Level 4 (9-10) a clear recommendation that is justified with economic theory, the information provided and its likely consequences for stakeholders; trade-offs and risks weighed. Level 3 (6-8) recommendation supported but justification partly developed. Level 2 (3-5) limited justification. Level 1 (1-2) recommendation asserted.

items.stem: Using an appropriate diagram, explain why a fall in price leads to an increase in total revenue when demand is price elastic.
items.answer: Diagram: elastic (relatively flat) demand; price falls from P1 to P2; quantity rises from Q1 to Q2. TR before = P1 × Q1 rectangle; after = P2 × Q2. Revenue lost (P1 − P2) × Q1 is smaller than revenue gained P2 × (Q2 − Q1), so TR rises.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: elastic (relatively flat) demand; price falls from P1 to P2; quantity rises from Q1 to Q2. TR before = P1 × Q1 rectangle; after = P2 × Q2. Revenue lost (P1 − P2) × Q1 is smaller than revenue gained P2 × (Q2 − Q1), so TR rises. Level 3 (6-8) mostly accurate with some development. Level 2 (3-5) limited explanation or diagram errors. Level 1 (1-2) little understanding.

items.stem: "Knowledge of PED is essential for firms setting prices." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: PED is valuable for pricing decisions, but estimates are imprecise and must be combined with knowledge of costs and rivals' behaviour.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows how revenue will change when price changes; helps target price discrimination; informs promotions and discounts. Arguments against: PED estimates are uncertain and change over time; competitors' reactions change outcomes; firms also consider costs, brand image and long-term objectives. Supported judgement: PED is valuable for pricing decisions, but estimates are imprecise and must be combined with knowledge of costs and rivals' behaviour. items.stem: Outline one way in which automatic enrolment in UK workplace pensions from 2012 shows default choices as a nudge.
items.answer: Employers had to enrol eligible workers automatically, who could opt out; participation in private-sector schemes rose from around 42% in 2012 to over 85% by 2019. Workers' inertia now worked in favour of saving, raising participation dramatically without compulsion.
items.markingKey: Context (Employers had to enrol eligible workers automatically, who could opt out; participation in private-sector schemes rose from around 42% in 2012 to over 85% by 2019.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Workers' inertia now worked in favour of saving, raising participation dramatically without compulsion. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to default choices as a nudge.

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, examine the extent to which government intervention is the best way to achieve equity.
items.answer: Intervention is usually necessary for equity, but its design matters to limit efficiency losses and government failure.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: markets distribute according to purchasing power, not need; taxes and transfers can redistribute effectively; governments can provide merit goods to all. Arguments against: intervention can reduce incentives and efficiency; government failure: poorly targeted policies; NGOs, communities and firms (CSR) also improve equity. Judgement: Intervention is usually necessary for equity, but its design matters to limit efficiency losses and government failure. Reward explicit use of the extract. items.stem: A country taxes income at 0% on the first $15,000, 25% on income from $15,000 to $50,000, and 45% on income above $50,000. Alessia earns $70,000. Calculate the tax paid, the average tax rate and the marginal tax rate, and state whether the system is progressive.
items.answer: Tax $17750; average rate 25.36%; marginal rate 45%; progressive
items.markingKey: Tax = 15,000×0% + 35,000×25% + 20,000×45% = 17750 [2]; average = 17750/70,000 = 25.36% [1]; marginal = 45% [1]; average rate rises with income ⇒ progressive.

items.stem: You are an adviser to a regional development agency. A minister argues that central planning can achieve faster development than a market economy. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: Planning may achieve rapid early industrialisation but sustained development has generally relied on markets combined with government action.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: state can mobilise savings for heavy industry quickly (USSR 1930s); can prioritise basic needs and equity. Counter-points: information and incentive problems create waste and shortages; lack of innovation and consumer choice; collapse of Soviet-style systems. Recommendation: Planning may achieve rapid early industrialisation but sustained development has generally relied on markets combined with government action.
